title: The pigeon and the peacock
hookLine: a pigeon today, or a peacock tomorrow?
carry: dharma bears fruit unseen, like a sown seed
tomorrow: the book's last lines aren't about love. who are they about?

lines: THE SURE THING, OR THE MAYBE?
cards: The paycheck job that starts Monday, or the unpaid internship that might lead somewhere. A group chat will split down the middle on that one, and somebody always types: take the sure thing.
In the Kama Sutra's opening, that voice has a name and a slogan. The Lokayatikas, thinkers who trust only what they can see, say a pigeon today is better than a peacock tomorrow.
And a copper coin you're sure of beats a gold coin you're not.

teach.h: THE LOKAYATIKAS: TAKE THE SURE THING.
teach.b: The book gives their case room, so hear it whole. Dharma promises its rewards later, somewhere no one has checked. Meanwhile it asks you to give things up now.
Why trade something real for a rumor? A pigeon in the hand can feed you tonight. That's a serious view, and the chapter states it in its own sharp words.
Vatsyayana answers that the teaching on dharma comes from scripture, and he treats it as trustworthy, not as a guess. Then he goes back to the field.

teach.h: A FARMER SOWS FOR AN UNSEEN CROP.
teach.b: A farmer puts seed in the ground for a crop he hasn't seen. Nobody calls that foolish. Acting now for a good you can't yet see is something people do every planting season.
This is a deep Hindu teaching about karma: actions bear fruit, often later and out of sight. Many families read their fasts, lamps and pujas this way, as seeds. So the two voices stand side by side.
One says: only what's in your hand is real.

teach.h: A SEED IN THE GROUND IS REAL TOO.
teach.b: The other says: so is a seed in the ground. And notice who stands where. The book of pleasure is the one defending the reward that can't be seen yet.

how: Readers of Indian philosophy know the Lokayatikas (also called Charvakas) as the school that trusted perception alone; the Kama Sutra's opening gives them a voice and answers them.

games.q: what does “the kama sutra's ethics chapter” mean?
o: an old opening that defends goods you can't see yet
a book of slogans about birds and old coins
a book that says take the sure thing every time

games.q: two voices in one chapter — tap the pairs.
p: sows for a crop he hasn't seen
trust only what they can see

s: the Kama Sutra sides with 'live for today'
here it argues the other way: a farmer sows for a crop he can't yet see.
the critics in this passage trust only what they can see
the Lokayatikas: take the pigeon, take the sure copper coin.
Vatsyayana mocks the Lokayatikas instead of answering them
he states their slogans sharply, then answers with scripture and the farmer's seed.

games.q: two cousins argue over graduation money: spend it now, or save it for later. give the 'spend it now' side its best case, in the Lokayatikas' words.
o: a sure copper coin beats a doubtful gold one.
pleasure is wrong, so give the money away.
the future is certain, so save every cent.
games.why: the Lokayatikas trust what's in hand: a pigeon today over a peacock tomorrow. Vatsyayana's answer is the farmer, who sows for a crop he can't see yet.

practice: Pick one choice in front of you where the sure thing pulls against the slow one. Say the sure thing's best case out loud, quietly, in one sentence, as if you believed it.
Then say the slow one's best case the same way, and sit with both sentences in the air, choosing nothing yet.

wordCard.voice: The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: here, the Lokayatikas' pigeon in the hand, answered by a farmer's seed.

orig.note: Sanskrit lokayata, the name of the school whose followers, the Lokayatikas, trust what they can see.

carryVoice: For the road: dharma bears fruit unseen, like a seed in the ground. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Kama Sutra 1.2 (the Lokayatika objection to dharma: the pigeon and the peacock, the copper and the gold coin; Vatsyayana's answer from scripture and the sowing of seed)
